extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, undergraduate mathematics instructors, curriculum developers, and mathematics education graduate students
extracted.subtask_description: Developing and validating a configuration/framework to analyze student approaches and difficulties with multiple representations of vectors in undergraduate mathematics, and using surveys/interviews to locate student difficulties on that configuration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Configuration of vector representations (two-axis classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: A configuration for analysis with two axes, ontological axis and epistemological axis: ontology concerns the nature/existence (e.g., geometric vs symbolic, concrete vs abstract); epistemology concerns the nature and scope of knowledge/ways of knowing (e.g., arithmetic→algebra, analytic→synthetic). Vector representations can be classified according to these two aspects to 'locate' a vector as a mathematical object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both axes to place representations and identify key jumps/transitions; the origin represents the jump from physics to mathematics (ontological and epistemological shifts). The configuration is a 'map of the territory' useful to organize thinking about teaching and learning the concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrows on a grid
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a representation of a vector in physics: an arrow in a physical context where physical directions (NSEW) and physical magnitudes (with units) are important, and measuring the arrow length on a grid corresponds to physical magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize that in this register vectors are tied to physical quantities and units; students may view arrows as depicting physical motion rather than abstract translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrows with axes and scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The first representation of a vector in mathematics closest to physics: an arrow placed on Cartesian coordinates with scales on each axis; direction described by origin and a point away from origin; length defines magnitude without physical units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This representation loses physical attachments (units) and treats points/objects as on a plane/3D space; useful when moving from physics intuition to mathematical representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrows with axes but no scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar to the above but exact length is not important; relative length matters and measuring length is not useful; origin's role as starting point of position vectors remains important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At this stage geometric objects are often interpreted as collections of points; emphasizes relations over measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrows without axes or scale
rubrics_metrics.description: No axes and no origin: direction and magnitude are not central; the focus is on the structure and relationships among several vectors (e.g., triangle vectors, angles, parallel/perpendicularity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages structural thinking about sums/differences of vectors rather than coordinate computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical column/coordinate form
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a basis, the tip of a position vector can be specified by a set of numbers forming a column or coordinate form (e.g., in R^2 or R^3 with an inner product).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This stage situates a vector as an element of finite-dimensional real vector space where numerical calculation and inner-product-based magnitude are meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Column/coordinate form with variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Column/coordinate form using variables and functions instead of fixed numbers (e.g., (f(x), g(x), h(x))), useful for parametrized curves or surfaces in multivariable calculus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bridges between concrete numerical coordinates and symbolic/functional descriptions; useful to examine parametrized objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Single letters or short symbols represent a column vector, arrow, or tuple (e.g., u, v, AB); structure of operations becomes easier to see though actual numerical calculation may not be possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length/magnitude exists only symbolically; strong connection to geometric representations often remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical n-tuple
rubrics_metrics.description: An extension of numerical coordinate form to four or higher dimensions (n-tuples); visual arrow analogy is harder but inner-product definition permits magnitude calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents a more abstract form; encourages thinking of vectors beyond 2D/3D geometric intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: N-tuple with variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of variables in an n-tuple to generalize numeric n-tuples (e.g., entries as variables), extending representational flexibility to higher dimensions with symbolic components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for abstract or parametric reasoning in higher-dimensional contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract elements in a vector space
rubrics_metrics.description: Vectors are elements of an abstract vector space defined by axioms; zero vectors, inverse vectors and operations are defined axiomatically without geometric or numeric content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represents the highest level of abstraction and ontological shift; stresses axiomatic structure over visualization or coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five important transitions (A–E)
rubrics_metrics.description: The framework identifies five key transitions among representations: (A) physics to mathematics, (B) arithmetic to algebraic, (C) analytic to synthetic, (D) geometric to symbolic, (E) concrete to abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These transitions mark epistemological and/or ontological jumps where student difficulties concentrate; use them as loci for designing tasks and diagnostic questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition (A): physics to mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Ontologically: shift from vectors as physical quantities with units to vectors as mathematical objects (directed line segments without units). Epistemologically: understanding equivalence relations (e.g., free vectors, position vectors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students often retain physical-attachment interpretations (e.g., an arrow must be near the object) and may fail to recognize translation equivalence; design tasks that highlight equivalence and translation across the plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition (B): arithmetic to algebra
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift from arithmetic (concrete numerical operations) to algebraic (variable thinking) reasoning, often occurring earlier in education but relevant to college-level contexts to ensure variable thinking persists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether students can use variable reasoning in vector contexts beyond simple numerics; tasks should probe proceptual understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition (C): analytic to synthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistemological shift between analytic (component/coordinate-based) and synthetic (geometric/structural) approaches; involves ontological reification/process-object encapsulation when moving to synthetic views.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synthetic approach expects structural insight (seeing sums/differences directly from geometric figures) rather than component calculations; tasks should reveal whether students default to analytic computations even when synthetic reasoning is more appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition (D): geometric object to symbolic object
rubrics_metrics.description: Ontological jump from geometric representations to symbolic/algebraic representations; at undergraduate level this implies understanding the difference between vector space and Euclidean coordinate space and the role of basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess students' grasp of basis and component-wise linear combinations; specifically probe whether students conflate point coordinates with vector coordinates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition (E): concrete to abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Shift toward abstract vector concepts (e.g., higher dimensions) where inner product/axiomatic definitions determine magnitude and structure rather than geometric intuition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that require generalization to 4D+ or abstract inner-product spaces to test whether students can detach from concrete geometric intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student approaches: Analytic vs Synthetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic approach: students use column/coordinate forms and decompose vectors into components to compute; Synthetic approach: students focus on geometric structures and holistic relationships to solve problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which approach students favor; measure flexibility and appropriateness of approach for given tasks (e.g., midpoint/parallelism theorem favors synthetic reasoning). The paper reports prevalence of analytic approach among surveyed students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semiotic registers and conversion asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Registers include graphical (arrows), table (columns), symbolic (axiomatic theory), and an additional 'physics' register; conversions between registers are asymmetric (example conversion success rates reported from Pvalopoulou's application of Duval's theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tasks that require translation between registers to diagnose where students fail; the asymmetry (e.g., low success converting graphical→symbolic) justifies locating representations on the configuration and targeting instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework features (interplay of ontological and epistemological aspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable feature: the framework should suggest that interplay between ontological and epistemological aspects is critical and that key transitions require both aspects simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing a framework/intervention, ensure it addresses both axes together rather than treating them separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework feature: distinguish analytic vs synthetic geometric representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework should distinguish and put emphasis on differences between analytic geometric representations and synthetic geometric representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this distinction to design tasks and curricula that deliberately cultivate synthetic (coordinate-free) reasoning as well as analytic skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework feature: distinguish physical vs mathematical representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework should distinguish between physical (embodied/physics) and mathematical (abstract) representations of vectors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction should explicitly address students' physical embodiment interpretations and help them reframe representations as mathematical objects when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework feature: embed parallel developments of symbolic and geometric representations with cognitive theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework should show, embed, and connect parallel developments of symbolic and geometric representations alongside cognitive development theories such as reification, process-object encapsulation, or APOS theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cognitive-developmental lenses when interpreting student responses and when sequencing instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framework feature: systematize transitions between representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Framework should systematize transitions between various representations of vectors to provide a 'map' for locating student difficulties and planning instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the configuration to plan instructional scaffolding that intentionally sequences transitions and supports reification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validation method for the framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate the configuration using literature review plus empirical data: task-based surveys, follow-up interviews, quantitative descriptive statistics and qualitative coding/analysis of responses and interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design survey tasks keyed to each transition/jump; analyze both which representation stages students can use and which transitions they struggle with; use cluster analyses and interviews to triangulate findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic criterion: locate student difficulties on transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify student difficulties by checking five important transitions and analyzing whether students can use representation stages and make transitions among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use targeted problems (e.g., translation, triangle midpoints) and follow-up interviews to reveal misinterpretations (e.g., treating translation arrows as local physical displacements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion: measure representational flexibility (use of few approaches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether students confine their understanding and use of vectors to a few preferred representations/approaches rather than showing flexibility across many representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey responses and task choices indicating dominance of analytic approach count as limited flexibility; aim to assess and encourage broad repertoire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and micro/macro complementarity (triple-component micro view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the configuration provides a macro/holistic view but is 'blurry' for individual thinking; complement with micro-analysis using triple components {representation content, semiotic register used, represented object}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating student cognition, combine macro mapping with detailed micro coding of individual utterances/representations to get a fuller picture.
